## 3. The evidence that moved it








**The most direct refutation on the microbiome thread is from May 2024, and it is
narrower than its title.** [38689063](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38689063/) (*Nat Med*) profiles the faecal
microbiota of 589 patients across colorectal cancer stages and compares against
up to 15 published studies totalling 4,439 subjects, using quantitative
profiling — absolute rather than relative abundance — with transit time, faecal
calprotectin and body mass index as covariates. Those three covariates explain
more variance than the diagnostic groups do, and under them the association
between *Fusobacterium nucleatum* and CRC stage dissolves. Six other taxa,
including *Parvimonas micra* and *Peptostreptococcus anaerobius*, survive the
same control and are named as targets worth keeping. So this is a confounding
result and not a null: it removes the field's most cited microbial target and
leaves the microbial account standing. It also finds that controls who meet the
criteria for colonoscopy but have no lesion are enriched for a dysbiotic
enterotype, which is a problem for every case-control design in the area.

!!! note "Corrected 2026-08-27"
    Two sentences have come out. The paper was read as challenging predicted
    microbial targets wholesale; six of them survive its own confounder control,
    and the corrected description is above. And it was said to predate "the
    thread's first recorded card by sixteen months" — the thread now opens in
    2023-01, so the arithmetic has been wrong since the backfill. A boast about a
    gap measured from the edge of what has been read has not once survived the
    edge moving.

**A myeloid target is removed and the outcome improves; another is removed and
the sign turns out to have been backwards.** [38758808](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38758808/) (*Sci Immunol*):
deleting TREM2 — a receptor this corpus already cards as nominated for
suppression on tumour macrophages ([37081148](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/37081148/), May 2023) — drives a
proinflammatory programme in intestinal macrophages, expands *Ruminococcus
gnavus* in the gut, and enhances anti-PD-1 tumour elimination, with TNF-producing
CD4 T cells expanding and migrating to the tumour bed. Gavaging wild-type mice
with *R. gnavus* reproduces the effect without touching TREM2 at all, which puts
the mechanism in the intestine rather than in the tumour. That is the
`suppressive-population-inversion` claim confirmed: remove the population, the
outcome improves. [38684922](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38684922/) (*Nat Immunol*) is the harder case and the
one filed as a refutation — sepsis-trained macrophages **promote** antitumoural
tissue-resident T cells, so a myeloid state assumed suppressive is protective and
depleting it would cost. The thread is running on both of its sides in May 2024.

!!! note "Corrected 2026-08-27"
    The TREM2 paper was carded `refutes`, and the old claim's closing sentence
    was "Removing a population improves the outcome" — which is this thread's
    claim word for word, filed as a refutation of it. On this thread `refutes` is
    reserved for inversions, where a population assumed suppressive turns out
    protective; deletion improving the outcome is the supporting case. The stance
    is now `supports`.

**And the same month supplies its mirror image.** [38664585](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38664585/) (*Nat Immunol*):
a dietary commensal microbe enhances antitumour immunity by activating tumour
macrophages to sequester iron. The same cell type, in the same journal, in the
same month, as an asset rather than a liability. That is the thread's actual
shape: not that suppressive populations are secretly good, but that the sign is
context-dependent and the field keeps assigning it globally.

## 4. Refutations

### (a) Landing on a tracked thread

The sepsis-macrophage paper above is the month's refutation on
`suppressive-population-inversion` and is filed there rather than here to avoid
double-counting; the TREM2 paper beside it supports that thread and is not a
refutation of anything.

[38227896](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38227896/) (*Cancer Discov*) refutes `immunotherapy-resistance`, and it
does so by being an excellent paper about the wrong compartment. Cancer cells
adaptively induce TREX1 through autocrine interferon and downstream STAT1, and
TREX1 degrades cytosolic DNA and so caps the cell's own STING-interferon
signalling before it can amplify. Inactivating TREX1 **in the cancer cell**
recruits T and NK cells, sensitises to NK-derived interferon-γ, and cooperates
with PD-1 blockade across mouse models. The thread's claim is that resistance is
being explained outside the tumour cell; the abstract locates the brake inside
it, five times over. The corpus already cards this exact shape as a refutation
([37553183](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/37553183/), August 2023, tumour-cell-intrinsic and not host STING).

!!! note "Corrected 2026-08-27"
    This entry read "[38227896](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38227896/) (*Cancer Discov*) is the supporting side of
    `immunotherapy-resistance`". The stance was set by the title's upbeat verb —
    "unleashes … promotes antitumour immunity" — rather than by where the paper
    puts the machinery, and it is now `refutes`.

### (b) Method credibility

The microbiome-confounders paper is the month's methodological result as well as
its biological one, which is the combination this corpus values most highly: the
reading and the finding are the same object. It does say that one particular
target is wrong, but the load-bearing claim is the general one: relative-abundance
profiling without covariate control cannot separate a microbial signal from
transit time, inflammation and body mass, and those are the variables that
explain most of the variance the field has been reading as disease.
